title: Why Can't You Drive Through the Darien Gap?

minor: 'In 1971-72, a British expedition' differs from the listed source, which says 1972. Add 1971 to the source entry or say 'in 1972'.
'Buses heading for Costa Rica' goes beyond the listed UNHCR/IOM entry, which says only 'buses north'. Say 'buses north' or add a source.
'Every attempt since 1510 to tame it' lumps the Santa María settlement and the Scots colony in with road plans, which they were not. 'Every attempt to settle or cross it' is more exact.
'400,000 pounds' should say pounds sterling, to avoid confusion with later currency.
'The rest had sailed away' compresses the 1699 abandonment, which is fine, but 'hundreds' (not 'many') matches the source.
'The Panama Canal cut the continent in two' is rhetorical. It is not wrong, but 'cut a waterway through the isthmus' is plainer.
The Guna Yala line is on the northern coast, not in the gap. Make clear it is context so viewers do not read it as inside the Darién.
The barbed-wire line 'meant to close some of them' states the government's intent in the narrator's voice. Attribute it aloud ('Panama said the wire was meant to...').

shots.title: *500,000* Walked

shots.vo: In 1698, 1,200 Scots landed here. Within a year, hundreds were dead.
The Pan-American Highway runs from Prudhoe Bay in Alaska to Ushuaia, near the southern tip of Argentina.
Drive south through Central America, and the last town on the road in Panama is Yaviza.
From there, the only way on is by boat up the river, or on foot.

shots.vo: The road starts again in northern Colombia, near Turbo, on the far side of the Gulf of Urabá.
Accounts of the gap differ, from about 97 kilometres to 106, depending on where each end is counted.
Along the border rise the Darién hills, topped by Cerro Tacarcuna at about 1,875 metres.
On the Colombian side, the Atrato River ends in a maze of swamps and marshes facing the gulf.
This is one of the rainiest regions on Earth.
Both sides are protected: Panama's Darién National Park and Colombia's Los Katíos are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
The park alone covers about 5,750 square kilometres, almost exactly the size of Brunei.

shots.vo: People live here too: Emberá, Wounaan and Guna communities, many of them reached mostly by river.

shots.vo: To the north, the Guna govern their own coastal territory, Guna Yala, under Panamanian law.
So drivers going south ship their cars in a container, from Colón in Panama to Cartagena in Colombia.
The missing road is about a three-hundredth of the whole highway, and nobody has ever finished it.
It is not for lack of trying: for five hundred years, plans to tame this jungle have failed here.
In 1510, Spanish settlers founded Santa María la Antigua del Darién, near the western shore of the Gulf of Urabá.

shots.vo: Historians describe it as an early Spanish town on the American mainland, though it lasted barely fourteen years.

shots.vo: In 1513, Vasco Núñez de Balboa set out from this coast and crossed the isthmus with Indigenous guides.
That September he saw the Pacific, the first European known to see it from the Americas.
But in 1519, the Spanish founded Panama City further west, and by 1524 Santa María was abandoned.
Gold and silver later crossed the isthmus far to the west, on the Camino Real between Panama City and Portobelo.
(map) In 1698, about 1,200 Scots sailed here to build a colony, New Caledonia, meant to link two oceans for trade.
Disease and hunger hit the settlers fast, and within a year many were dead and the rest had sailed away.

shots.vo: A second wave arrived, Spain laid siege, and in 1700 the colony surrendered for good.
Seven years later, Scotland and England merged into one kingdom, and many historians see the Darien loss as one reason.

shots.vo: In November 1903, Panama broke away from Colombia, with the support of the United States.
In 1923, at a conference in Santiago, Chile, the American states agreed to plan one highway to join them.

map.label: 1923 plan: one line, Alaska to Chile

shots.vo: A year later, a treaty signed in 1924 fixed the Panama–Colombia border across the Darién; it runs about 339 kilometres today.
Over the following decades it was built country by country, until the pavement reached the edge of the Darién.
In the early 1970s, the United States agreed to pay two-thirds of the cost of the Darién section.
In 1971-72, a British expedition hauled two Range Rovers through the gap; it was a long, slow crossing of cutting and winching.

shots.vo: Then in 1975, environmental groups sued in a US court, and a judge stopped the work.

document.highlight: Work on the Darién Gap highway halted pending a full environmental review

shots.vo: One worry was cattle: foot-and-mouth disease was present in South America, and the jungle kept it out of the north.
North and Central America are still free of the disease, and officials count the gap as part of that barrier.

shots.vo: So the highway stopped at Yaviza, but the empty gap was about to fill with people.
In 2021, about 134,000 people crossed on foot; in 2023, Panama counted 520,085, its highest ever.
Most came from Venezuela, followed by Ecuador, Haiti and even China, on journeys that began thousands of kilometres away.
Many start in Necoclí, take a boat across the gulf to Acandí or Capurganá, then walk into the hills.
Most take between four and ten days, crossing rivers, steep mud and forest.

shots.vo: UNICEF says more than 113,000 of the people who crossed in 2023 were children.

shots.vo: On the Colombian side, Human Rights Watch reported that an armed group, the Gulf Clan, controls the routes and charges fees.
In Panama, walkers reach reception stations such as Lajas Blancas, then board buses heading for Costa Rica.
In July 2024, Panama's new president, José Raúl Mulino, signed a deal with Washington to fly migrants home, with the US paying about $6 million.
(map) The government also strung barbed wire across several jungle paths, meant to close some of them.

shots.vo: Crossings fell to about 302,000 in 2024, still more than twice the total of 2021.
Then in early 2025, crossings were reported down by more than 90 percent, a fall officials and analysts link to harder US policy.

shots.vo: Some people began moving the other way, south by boat along Panama's Caribbean coast toward Colombia.
Panama's government describes itself as a transit country.
Rights groups argue that closing paths pushes people onto hidden trails, further from help.
So which is safer for everyone: a gap that stays shut, or one that is finally crossed?
Scenario one: build the road. In the 1970s, Washington and Panama backed it to join two continents by land.
Some officials and business groups in Colombia and Panama argue trucks could then carry goods and medicines overland, at lower cost.
They add that a road would finally bring clinics, schools and other services to the river villages.

shots.vo: On the map, that road would cut through two World Heritage parks and Indigenous lands on both sides.
Emberá and Guna leaders have long said they fear a road would bring loggers, ranchers and settlers.

shots.vo: Their example is next door: along the road Panama already built toward Yaviza, much of the forest became pasture.
Scenario two: go around by sea. From 2014, a car ferry ran from Colón to Cartagena.
The ferry stopped about a year later, and drivers went back to shipping their cars in containers.

shots.vo: Scenario three: leave it as it is, the parks protected and the border watched from both sides.
That keeps the forest standing, but some analysts warn the walkers could return if policies change.

shots.vo: If you could decide, which would you choose: the road, the ferry, or the jungle left alone?
The Darién Gap is not a road nobody could build. Every attempt since 1510 to tame it has left it unfinished.
